Chip thread: 'chip exports have carried growth through recent slowdowns' was softened to 'have become a growing source of growth', because the cited passages say only that the chip focus boosts growth.

growth_story.headline: Korea climbed from poor to rich on decades of fast catch-up; since 2008 growth has eased to 2.4 percent a year as catch-up fades and the workforce ages.
growth_story.arc: Korea's income per person rose from about 1,038 dollars in 1960 to about 37,470 in 2025 (in constant dollars), and 2025 is its highest level yet. Since 1990 growth has come in three eras: 7.4 percent a year in 1990–1997, 4.6 in 1998–2007 and 2.4 in 2008–2025. The first era was the late stage of a long catch-up that the OECD traces to market-friendly reforms in the 1960s, with fixed investment between 35.1 and 38.4 percent of GDP every year from 1990 to 1997. The 1997–98 crisis ended that era: income per person fell 5.6 percent in 1998 and rebounded 10.8 percent in 1999, while investment fell to 30.1 percent of GDP in 1998 and has stayed between 28.3 and 31.9 since. Since 2008 growth has slowed again; the sources point to less room for catch-up as Korea reached the OECD's average income, and to productivity gains that faded in the 2010s. Growth over the last decade averaged 2.2 percent a year, down from 3.2 in the decade before, and the sources now add an ageing workforce, a building slump and a heavy reliance on chips.

threads.title: The 1997 crisis
threads.text: When the Asian crisis hit in 1997, Korea's big family-run business groups (chaebol) were deep in debt and its banks were weighed down by bad loans. Income per person fell 5.6 percent in 1998 and bounced back 10.8 percent in 1999, but investment never regained its old share: it dropped from 35.1 percent of GDP in 1997 to 30.1 in 1998.

threads.title: Catch-up runs its course
threads.text: Market-friendly reforms in the 1960s started decades of very fast growth. As Korea reached the OECD's average income there was less to catch up on, and productivity gains that had added steadily to growth since the 1980s faded in the 2010s.

threads.title: Ageing and a shrinking workforce
threads.text: Korea has the world's lowest fertility rate, and its working-age population peaked in 2019. The OECD expects the labour force to start shrinking as a share of the population within a few years, with large consequences for growth and public finances.

threads.title: Riding the chip cycle
threads.text: Korea is a world leader in advanced chips, and chip exports have become a growing source of growth. The OECD notes that this focus lifts growth but also leaves the economy more exposed to outside shocks and to swings in the chip cycle.

since_last_year.text: Growth slowed in early 2025 amid political uncertainty after the martial law declaration of late 2024 and uncertainty over global trade policy. Income per person grew 1.1 percent in 2025, the slowest since 2020. Consumer confidence improved after the 2025 election, and by mid-2026 the OECD described chip exports driving a recovery while construction and other factories lagged, until conflict in the Middle East broke out.

growth_story.tension: The IMF says Korea's potential growth "has slowed at a faster pace relative to its peers", but the data show Korea still growing faster than its structural peers. Over 2016–2025 its income per person grew 2.2 percent a year, against a peer median of 1.1. That ranks it 3 of 11 and puts it 0.6 standard deviations above what its income level would predict. Both can be true: Korea slowed faster, but it started from a much higher growth rate.
